label: Action
note: Exit ticket: What verb hides inside action?

deep.summary: What you learn: -tion / -ion often turns a verb-like stem into a noun naming an act, process, or result—compare “act” vs “action.” Spelling varies (decide → decision) but the pattern is common in academic vocabulary.

etymology.origin: Stem meaning “do”—same family as the verb act.
Builds abstract nouns from many Latinate stems.

label: National
note: Exit ticket: Use national in a sentence as an adjective describing something tied to a whole country.

deep.summary: What you learn: -al frequently makes adjectives meaning “related to ___.” Here it turns nation into “about a nation.” You’ll see the same ending on many school-book adjectives (cultural, logical).

label: Happiness
note: Exit ticket: Why does the vowel spelling shift before -ness (happy → happiness)?

deep.summary: What you learn: -ness turns many adjectives into abstract nouns naming a state or quality: “being ___.” English often shortens or adjusts the last consonants/vowels of the adjective first (happy → happi-)—that bump is a spelling pattern worth collecting, not guessing randomly.

spelling.note: The y drops before vowel-initial -ness—similar idea to other suffix joins.

label: Movement
note: Exit ticket: Name another -ment noun built from a verb you use in science class.

deep.summary: What you learn: -ment builds nouns—often “the result or process of ___ing.” Compare verb move with noun movement. You’ll meet this suffix constantly in history and science readings.

etymology.origin: Nominalizing suffix—pairs with many Latinate verb bases.

label: Readable
note: Exit ticket: Say readable in plain kid English (“can be ___ed”). Then try visible: same suffix job with a Latinate stem.

deep.summary: What you learn: -able (and its cousin -ible after certain stems) builds adjectives meaning “can be ___ed” or “worthy of being ___ed.” Same logic behind visible, even when the stem isn’t an everyday English verb by itself.
deep.formation: Teachable rule of thumb: if you can paraphrase with “can be …,” you’re probably in -able / -ible territory.

label: Hopeless
note: Exit ticket: Explain hopeless without using “less”—what does it say about hope?

deep.summary: What you learn: -less builds “without ___.” Contrast with -ful on the same base when possible (hopeful / hopeless)—meaning flips in a teachable way.
deep.tense: Adjective describing a state or outlook.

label: Invisible
note: Exit ticket: Match the assimilated prefix to the first letter of the base in illegal, impossible, irregular.

deep.summary: What you learn: This is the “not” family of in- (with spellings im-, il-, ir- to match the next consonant). It negates what the base says—here, “not visible.”
deep.formation: Compare to separate lesson on in- meaning “in / on / toward” — spelling overlaps, meaning differs; context decides.

label: Disconnect
note: Exit ticket: Find a word where the Latin prefix surfaces as dif- (difference family) and say what the base means.

deep.summary: What you learn: dis- often marks reversal or separation (disagree, disappear). Stacked on connect (= con- + nect = “bind together”), the result disconnect = “undo the binding-together.”

etymology.origin: Apart / negation / undoing—sense depends on the base verb.

deep.formation: Three layers stacked outward: nect (bind) → con + nect (bind together) → dis + con + nect (undo the binding-together).

label: Nonsense
note: Exit ticket: How is non- different from un- in tone—scientific labels (nonfiction) vs everyday negation?

deep.summary: What you learn: non- builds “not / other than” on nouns and adjectives—common in school genres (nonfiction, nonprofit). It often feels more technical than everyday un-.
deep.tense: Here nonsense is a noun naming “no-meaning talk.”

label: Import
note: Exit ticket: Contrast “not” in- with this “in/into” sense—what does import literally suggest about movement?

deep.summary: What you learn: This is the “into / toward” family—not negation. Import is literally “carry in.” Same letters as negation in- in other words, so you must read base meaning + context.
deep.formation: Keep two mental boxes: in- = not vs in- = in/into — spelling alone won’t separate them.

label: Misunderstand
note: Exit ticket: Build another mis- word and say what went wrong in the meaning (“badly / wrongly”).

children.gloss: verb stem: stand / take a position

deep.summary: What you learn: Mis- marks error or bad execution (misprint, mislead). It’s not “not” exactly—it’s “wrongly.” Stacked on understand (Old English “stand among / beneath”), misunderstand = “take the wrong stand on a meaning.”

etymology.origin: Wrong / astray—pairs well with classroom talk about misconceptions.
Old English standan 'take a position'—same family as the literal verb.

deep.formation: Three layers: stand → under + stand (take a position among) → mis + under + stand (take the wrong position).

label: Preview
note: Exit ticket: Name something you preview before a test or trip.

deep.summary: What you learn: Pre- sets time early—before the main event (predict, prepare). Pair it mentally with post- (“after”) when you meet opposites in texts.

label: International
note: Exit ticket: What does inter- add compared to plain national?

deep.summary: What you learn: Inter- signals “between / among” (interact, intersect). Here it widens national to cross-border relations.
deep.formation: Nested layers: nation → national → international — each suffix wraps the bigger bundle.

label: Forecast
note: Exit ticket: Connect fore- to everyday “before” words (before, forward).

deep.summary: What you learn: Fore- points ahead in time or position (foreshadow, forward). Forecast is “throw/cast the outcome ahead of time” in a metaphor English keeps alive in weather talk.
deep.tense: Can be verb or noun depending on sentence.

label: Decode
note: Exit ticket: When does de- mean “remove / reverse” vs “down / away”? Compare decode and deflate.

deep.summary: What you learn: De- often reverses an action or pulls something “off/down” (defrost, deactivate). In reading class, decode names the flip side of encode.

etymology.origin: Reversal / removal — sense depends on the base.

label: Transport
note: Exit ticket: List two other trans- words that mean “across” in science or social studies.

deep.summary: What you learn: Trans- marks crossing—space (transport), boundaries (translate), or states (transform). The stable anchor is “movement across.”

etymology.origin: Carry — same root thread as import, portable.

label: Antifreeze
note: Exit ticket: How does anti- differ from non- in attitude (antivirus vs nonstick)?

tree.gloss: noun: chemical that lowers freezing point

deep.summary: What you learn: Anti- sets up opposition—against a thing or process (antibiotic, anticlockwise). In compounds it tightens what kind of substance or force you mean.
deep.tense: Noun in science/chemistry contexts; stress pattern helps listening comprehension.

label: Connect
note: Exit ticket: What does “with / together” add to the stem in connect compared to nect alone (not a standalone English word)?

deep.summary: What you learn: Con- (also com-, col-, cor- before certain letters) often means “with” or “together.” Here it names joining with something else.
deep.formation: Assimilated spelling matches the next consonant—same prefix family, easier pronunciation.

label: Advance
note: Exit ticket: Where else do you see ad- shortened or assimilated (approach, assign)?

deep.summary: What you learn: Latin ad- often means “to / toward,” with spellings like ac-, af-, al- before certain letters. In school texts it shows up on formal verbs (adhere, attract).

label: Inform
note: Exit ticket: List another word where form means “shape” (transform, uniform).

deep.summary: What you learn: The bound stem form carries “shape.” Here the metaphor is “put shape into someone’s mind”—tell them. Related words reuse the same stem (transform, reform).

etymology.origin: Shape / structure — not usually a free morpheme in these Latinate builds.

label: Export
note: Exit ticket: Compare import and export using “carry in/out.”

deep.summary: What you learn: port = carry. Economics and geography reuse it constantly (import, portable, transport). Spotting it speeds decoding of long textbook words.

etymology.origin: Carry — stable meaning across many compounds.

label: Interrupt
note: Exit ticket: What does corrupt mean if rupt is “break”?

deep.summary: What you learn: Rupt signals breaking—same stem as erupt, corrupt. Interrupt is “break between” someone’s speech or focus.

label: Attract
note: Exit ticket: Where else do you see tract meaning pull (tractor, traction)?

deep.summary: What you learn: Tract = draw/pull. Physical and metaphor uses overlap (attract attention). Hook this stem to machinery words (tractor) for memory.

label: Describe
note: Exit ticket: Link description and manuscript to writing meanings.

children.gloss: marker e (signals long i; protects scrib)

deep.summary: What you learn: The scrib/script family names writing—describe literally “writes down” what something is like. The silent -e at the end is a marker (it cues the long /aɪ/ in scribe); it isn’t a separate meaning, but the SWI word sum keeps it visible: de + scrib + e. Related nouns use -tion (description) and the e is dropped before the vowel suffix.

spelling.note: Marker e protects the long-i pronunciation and disappears when a vowel-initial suffix joins (describing, description).

deep.tense: Verb — classroom staple for evidence-based writing.

label: Inspect
note: Exit ticket: Collect three words that mean “looking” with this root (spectator, suspicious).

deep.summary: What you learn: Spect/spec = look/watch—same spine as spectacle, suspicious, perspective. Prefix tells you how the looking aims.

label: Construct
note: Exit ticket: What noun names the building process (construction)?

deep.summary: What you learn: Struct/stru names building—think structure, instruct, destroy (literally “un-build”). Science and history readings pile these words together.

label: Dictionary
note: Exit ticket: Explain dictionary as something relating to (-ary) the abstract “saying” built on dict + -ion (diction).

tree.gloss: noun: reference book of words and their senses

children.gloss: suffix: abstract noun — act, process, or result

deep.summary: What you learn: Dictionary sums as dict + -ion + -ary: a thing relating to (-ary) the diction (“what is said”) built on dict (“say/speak”) — a book of word-sayings.

etymology.origin: Latin dīcere ‘say, speak’ — same spine as verdict, dictate, predict.
Nominalizing suffix: here names the abstract noun family (diction / what is said).
Relational suffix — pertaining to the base noun.

label: Contradict
note: Exit ticket: Paraphrase contradict without using the word — use “against” and “say.”

tree.gloss: verb: say against; assert the opposite of

deep.summary: What you learn: contra- means against; dict means say. Together: “say against” — opposing a claim in words.

etymology.origin: Latin ‘say, speak’ — same base as dictionary and predict.

label: Uniform
note: Exit ticket: How does uni- (one) change the meaning of form (shape)?

deep.summary: What you learn: Uniform = uni (one) + form (shape) — literally “one shape,” so parts match instead of varying.

etymology.origin: Latin forma ‘shape, figure’ — same base as information, transform.

label: Refer
note: Exit ticket: How does refer connect to carrying an idea “back” to something?

deep.summary: What you learn: Fer carries/bears—same spine as transfer, fertile. Refer is “carry attention back” to a source.

label: Transmit
note: Exit ticket: Compare mission (something sent) with submit (send under).

deep.summary: What you learn: Mit/miss = send—think mission, missile, submit. Science words reuse it for signals (transmit light).

label: Conduct
note: Exit ticket: Where does a science teacher use conduct as “lead” vs “behavior”?

deep.summary: What you learn: Duc/duct = lead—same spine as produce, reduce. Context toggles between leading electricity/music and leading oneself (behavior).
deep.tense: Noun vs verb stress differs in speech—good listening practice.

label: Perfect
note: Exit ticket: Explain why perfect feels like “made all the way through.”

deep.summary: What you learn: Fac/fect/fic names making/doing—factory, manufacture, fiction. Perfect is “thoroughly made / finished.”
deep.formation: Many advanced adjectives hide this stem behind vowel shifts—collect families instead of memorizing alone.

label: Maintain
note: Exit ticket: Link contain, sustain, and tenant to holding.

deep.summary: What you learn: Tain/ten/tin holds—contain, sustain, maintenance. If you know “hold,” you can hang more textbook verbs on the stem.

spelling.note: Not spelled like “main street” + random ending—the second chunk is the bound stem “hold.”

label: Receive
note: Exit ticket: Compare accept and except—don’t mix spellings or meanings.

deep.summary: What you learn: The ceive/cept family is “take/catch”—receive, accept, except (different prefixes steer meaning). Spelling groups belong together for study cards.
deep.formation: Collect minimal pairs with different prefixes on the same stem.

label: Assistant
note: Exit ticket: Who “stands by” to help in a classroom or lab?

deep.summary: What you learn: Sist/stat/stit stands—assist (stand to), consist, station. An assistant “stands by” to help.

label: Position
note: Exit ticket: Connect compose and deposit to “place.”

deep.summary: What you learn: Pon/pos/posit places things—position, compose (place together), opposition (place against). Social studies and science reuse this stem.

etymology.origin: Place / put — bound stem inside many classroom words.

label: Apply
note: Exit ticket: What’s folded toward what in application (idea → form)?

deep.summary: What you learn: Plic/ply folds—apply (fold toward), complicated (folded together). Abstract but high payoff once students collect the family.
deep.tense: Verb with several sentence frames—reading class uses ‘apply evidence.’

label: Biography
note: Exit ticket: Find another graph word in math or science class (paragraph, photograph).

deep.summary: What you learn: Greek graph/gram writes or records—photograph, grammar, diagram. Biography writes a life.

label: Biotic
note: Exit ticket: In ecology, what is the difference between biotic (living) and abiotic (nonliving)?

deep.summary: What you learn: Biotic is built from bio (life) + -tic (relating to). In science reading it helps you spot “living / life” language quickly.
deep.tense: Adjective in science/ecology; often paired with abiotic in classroom talk.

label: Biology
note: Exit ticket: Name two school subjects ending in -ology.

deep.summary: What you learn: Biology is built from two meaningful pieces: bio (life) and -logy (study of). Together they mean the study of life. The same pattern shows up in geology, psychology, zoology, and more.

etymology.origin: Life — the same combining chunk as in biography and antibiotic.
Study or science of — from Greek *logos* ‘reason, word’; names a school subject or field.

label: Geology
note: Exit ticket: In one sentence, what does geology study?

deep.summary: What you learn: Geology = geo (earth, ground) + -logy (study of). It is the science that studies rocks, landforms, and how the planet changes over time.

etymology.origin: Earth / land — Greek root you also see in geography and geometry.
Study of — turns the topic into a field-of-study word.

label: Psychology
note: Exit ticket: Without looking it up, what two morphemes make psychology?

deep.summary: What you learn: Psychology splits into psych (mind — from Greek *psukhē*, breath / soul / mind) and -ology (study of). So the word means the study of the mind — thoughts, feelings, and behavior. English spells it psych + ology, not *psychlogy*.

etymology.origin: Mind / spirit — the combining form you also see in psychic and psychiatrist.
Study of — same morpheme as -logy; the o links the stem to the suffix in spelling.

label: Zoology
note: Exit ticket: What does zoo mean in zoology (hint: not just the park)?

deep.summary: What you learn: Zoology = zoo (animal — from Greek *zōion* ‘living being’) + -logy (study of). It is the branch of biology that focuses on animals — their bodies, behavior, and diversity. A zoo (short for zoological garden) uses the same animal root.

etymology.origin: Animal — Greek *zōion*; connects to zoo and zoological.
Study of — names the science or school subject built on the first chunk.

label: Etymology
note: Exit ticket: Why does etymology fit this page’s name (morphology / analysis of words)?

deep.summary: What you learn: Etymology = etym (true or original sense — Greek *etumos* ‘true’) + -ology (study of). So it means the study of where words came from and what they really meant at first — exactly what you do when you prove a word sum with evidence.

etymology.origin: True / original meaning — the ‘truth’ half of the compound.
Study of — the discipline suffix; same family as -logy in biology.
